Robert Louis Stevenson. A Scottish author and adventurer whose imaginative tales of mystery, adventure, and psychological terror defined Victorian literature. Born in eighteen fifty and dying of tuberculosis in Samoa in eighteen ninety-four, he produced works of enduring cultural force, including Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde and Treasure Island, that explore dual natures and the romantic allure of transgression.

He wrote Treasure Island, one of the first novels to define the modern pirate adventure genre. Serialized initially in a boys' magazine, it features iconic figures like Long John Silver and young Jim Hawkins.

Stevenson created Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde, a novella about a doctor's chemical experiment that unleashes his repressed evil self, becoming a touchstone for psychological horror and the duality of human nature. He also wrote Kidnapped, a novel of adventure and identity set in post-Jacobite Scotland, featuring the memorable character Alan Breck Stewart and exploring themes of loyalty, exile, and the Highland clearances.

He suffered from chronic tuberculosis throughout his life, which forced periods of travel and confinement that shaped both his work and his wanderlust. Illness becomes a recurring theme in his fiction.

He settled in Samoa at age forty, where he lived among the local population and wrote essays and stories that revealed deep respect for Pacific cultures. The Samoans called him Tusitala, "the teller of tales," honoring his storytelling gifts.

He pioneered a prose style that balanced Victorian propriety with gothic sensibility, blending adventure narrative with philosophical introspection and moral ambiguity that influenced modernist writers.

He wrote The Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde as a novella of fewer than thirty thousand words, yet created one of literature's most enduring explorations of morality, addiction, and split personality.
